The Science

A Deeper Look Inside Tirzepatide

Understanding the dual-action mechanism that makes Tirzepatide one of the most studied weight-loss medications available.

What is Tirzepatide?

Tirzepatide is a first-in-class dual agonist for two natural gut hormones, GIP and GLP-1. It tells your brain you are full and slows stomach emptying.1

As routines get busy and stress builds, many people find it harder to stay consistent with nutrition, movement, and daily habits. Tirzepatide works with your body’s own systems to regulate appetite and improve metabolic function, and it is stronger than semaglutide in clinical study settings.3

At MedMethod Direct, tirzepatide is only considered after a clinical evaluation, with ongoing monitoring, dosage guidance, and continued support if prescribed.

Studies examine Tirzepatide’s role in:

Weight Loss

20.9%

Average body weight reduction over 72 weeks on the 15 mg dose, compared with 3.1% on placebo, in 2,539 adults with obesity or overweight.

Ref: SURMOUNT-1, NEJM 2022

Keeping Weight Off

25.3%

Total weight reduction at 88 weeks for participants who stayed on tirzepatide. Those switched to placebo after week 36 regained 14.0%.

Ref: SURMOUNT-4, JAMA 2024

Compared With Semaglutide

20.2%

Average weight reduction over 72 weeks with tirzepatide versus 13.7% with semaglutide, in a head-to-head trial of 751 adults with obesity.

Ref: SURMOUNT-5, NEJM 2025

Aronne LJ, Horn DB, le Roux CW, et al. Tirzepatide as Compared with Semaglutide for the Treatment of Obesity. N Engl J Med. 2025;393(1):26-36.

These trials studied FDA-approved tirzepatide. Compounded tirzepatide was not evaluated in these trials. Individual results vary.

Common Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Tirzepatide is a first-in-class dual agonist for two natural gut hormones, GIP and GLP-1. It stimulates insulin release when blood sugar is high, reduces glucose production by the liver, slows gastric emptying so you feel fuller longer, and targets the brain areas that regulate appetite and cravings.
By mimicking GLP-1 and GIP, tirzepatide tells your brain you are full, slows stomach emptying, reduces hunger, and helps regulate blood sugar. The combined effect is eating less and feeling full, which creates the calorie deficit that drives weight loss.
No referral is needed. You can begin by completing our online intake form. From there, our team will connect you with a provider to discuss your options and determine the most appropriate path forward.
Your provider will guide you on the exact dosing schedule. Compounded tirzepatide is typically taken once weekly by injection. Follow your provider’s instructions closely for the best results and minimal side effects.
MedMethod Direct operates as a direct-pay practice and does not bill insurance directly. Some patients may be able to use HSA or FSA funds. Contact us for details about payment options.
We provide continued follow-up care throughout your program. This includes progress monitoring, plan adjustments as needed, answers to your questions, and ongoing encouragement.

What medications do you currently take?

Include prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, and supplements — with the dosage if you know it. Some medications interact with tirzepatide, so your care team needs the full list.

Do you have any allergies?

Medication allergies especially — and what reaction you had, if you remember it.

Do you have severe stomach or digestion problems, or gastroparesis?

Gastroparesis means your stomach empties too slowly. Tirzepatide also slows digestion, so this changes whether it’s right for you.

Do you have kidney disease?

Including reduced kidney function or dialysis.

Do you have diabetic eye disease or retinopathy?

Rapid blood-sugar improvement can temporarily affect diabetic eye disease, so your provider needs to know.

Have you had weight-loss surgery?

For example gastric bypass, gastric sleeve, or a lap band.

Pregnancy plans & contraception

Tirzepatide isn’t used during pregnancy, and it can make birth control pills less effective because it slows digestion.

Are you planning to become pregnant in the next year?
